strengths: The core idea—moving a Merlin–Arthur prover-verifier game from pixels to a compact concept representation—is intuitive, potentially useful, and offers a plausible way to improve scalability and human readability.

The evaluation covers synthetic compositional data and two natural-image benchmarks. Reporting results over 20 seeds for CLEVR-Hans and 10 seeds for CIFAR-100/ImageNet is stronger than the common single-run evaluation.

The reported predictive results are promising: NCV substantially improves over Pixel-MAC on CIFAR-100 and ImageNet and over the stated CBM baseline on most datasets. The mask-size and prover-architecture ablations on CLEVR-Hans provide some useful sensitivity analysis.

The manuscript is generally well organized and clearly explains the high-level architecture, training game, completeness metric, and empirical soundness metric. It also honestly acknowledges dependence on concept quality, inherited CLIP biases, training instability, and the absence of multiclass theoretical guarantees.
The shortcut experiments include an appropriate nonlinear-CBM comparison, helping separate some benefits of the game from the benefit of nonlinear prediction alone.
weaknesses: The central faithfulness/verifiability claim is not established. Merlin observes the complete concept vector and chooses a mask whose index pattern is visible to Arthur. With 32 selected indices among 10,000 concepts, this pattern is an enormous communication channel that can encode the predicted class independently of the selected concepts' semantic values. No control randomizes concept values, hides indices, constrains class-conditional mask information, or tests whether Arthur actually uses concept meanings rather than the mask pattern. Consequently, sparse named concepts are not necessarily faithful evidence.

The reported near-100% “soundness” is only performance against one learned Morgana, not a certificate or worst-case guarantee. Morgana may fail to discover stronger masks, and the verifier can potentially recognize Morgana's mask distribution and reject it. The paper provides neither optimization diagnostics nor attacks with stronger, restarted, or independently optimized adversaries. Calling these numbers “formal,” “certifiable,” or “soundness guarantees” is therefore unsupported, especially since the conclusion admits that existing theory does not cover this high-dimensional multiclass setting.

Interpretability is supported only by a few qualitative, synthetic CLEVR examples selected from three classes. There is no quantitative concept-faithfulness metric, human evaluation, systematic sample analysis, or explanation study on CIFAR-100/ImageNet. The paper therefore does not substantiate its broader claims of human-readable explanations on natural images, particularly for an automatically mined 10,000-phrase LAION vocabulary.

The principal CBM comparison is confounded. On natural images, NCV receives dense CLIP similarity features while the CBM receives separately optimized sparse SpLiCE encodings; thus the accuracy difference cannot be attributed to nonlinear prover-verifier reasoning. Moreover, Appendix A.3 calls the baseline linear but then states that it uses a 512-unit hidden layer. Missing matched controls include a nonlinear MLP on the identical dense CLIP-Sim representation, Merlin-only sparse selection, and NCV without adversarial training.

The shortcut evidence is limited and partly contradicts the broad claim of intrinsic mitigation. With 0% clean CLEVR-Hans7 data, NCV's validation-test gap (6.15) is worse than the linear CBM's (5.10); on CLEVR-Hans3, NCV has both a worse gap and lower test accuracy than the nonlinear CBM. Improvements mainly emerge after clean examples are introduced, and no natural-image shortcut or standard distribution-shift benchmark is evaluated.

Reproducibility is inadequate for the central game. The exact modified Morgana loss is omitted, hard top-k selection is described as differentiable without specifying its gradient estimator or relaxation, update schedules and game-optimization details are incomplete, the CLIP model/checkpoint is unspecified, and no code or artifact availability statement is given. Main results use mask size 32, while the natural-image ablation tables report only 4, 8, 16, and 64 and only train/validation results, so the central test numbers cannot be traced to the appendix.

The claimed scalability is inferred from accuracy rather than measured: there are no runtime, memory, convergence, or compute comparisons. Training 100 ImageNet epochs over 10 seeds with three networks is substantial, yet hardware and computational cost are not reported.

Presentation contains consequential inconsistencies: gamma is declared nonnegative although the convex weighting formula requires gamma in [0,1]; the CBM architecture is inconsistently described; and multiple references contain placeholder arXiv identifiers or malformed author fields. Ethical limitations of CLIP/LAION are mentioned appropriately, but no concrete bias evaluation is provided despite positioning the method for high-stakes use.

Overall, the combination is moderately original and the empirical accuracies are interesting, but the unaddressed mask-channel confound and purely empirical learned-adversary metric undermine the paper's defining claims of faithful, verifiable reasoning. These are central methodological issues requiring new controls and a substantial reframing, rather than minor revisions.

strengths: The paper identifies a useful problem: pixel-space prover-verifier games scale poorly and produce explanations that are difficult to interpret, while linear concept bottlenecks can lack expressivity. Combining concept encodings with a nonlinear Merlin-Arthur classifier is a sensible direction.

The evaluation spans two controlled CLEVR-Hans benchmarks and two natural-image benchmarks, with results averaged over 20 seeds for CLEVR-Hans and 10 seeds for CIFAR-100/ImageNet. NCV obtains strong completeness on CLEVR-Hans and CIFAR-100; for example, Table 1 reports 98.92% on CLEVR-Hans3 and 83.32% on CIFAR-100.

The mask-size and selector-architecture ablations provide some useful evidence about sparsity-performance tradeoffs. The shortcut experiments also include a nonlinear CBM control and multiple clean-data ratios rather than relying on a single confounding condition.

The manuscript is generally readable, clearly organized, and includes substantial training and architecture details. Its limitations section appropriately acknowledges dependence on concept quality, three-agent optimization cost and instability, and inherited CLIP biases.
weaknesses: The central verifiability claim is not established. Reported soundness is merely performance against the particular learned Morgana adversary, not a certificate against all allowed feature selections or a formal multiclass guarantee. The paper presents no theorem or attack-strength evaluation, and explicitly concedes that existing information-theoretic guarantees only cover binary classification under specific assumptions. Terms such as “certified,” “formal verifiability,” and “soundness guarantees” are therefore overstated.

Near-perfect soundness is difficult to interpret because either a correct prediction or rejection counts as success. The paper reports neither rejection rates nor selective accuracy/coverage under adversarial selections. A verifier that distinguishes the two provers' mask distributions and rejects Morgana systematically could attain nearly perfect soundness without verifying meaningful evidence. Evaluation against independently trained, restarted, or stronger adversaries is also absent.

The main accuracy comparison is seriously confounded. On CIFAR-100 and ImageNet, NCV uses dense CLIP-Sim features whereas the CBM baseline uses sparse SpLiCE features, so the comparison simultaneously changes representation, sparsification procedure, classifier, and PVG training. The necessary controls—an MLP on the same dense CLIP-Sim vector, top-k selection without Morgana, and Merlin-only training—are missing. Consequently, the gains cannot be attributed to the proposed prover-verifier mechanism.

The characterization of the natural-image CBM baseline is internally inconsistent. It is repeatedly called a linear classifier, but Appendix A.3 says that it has a 512-unit hidden layer. This ambiguity directly affects the claimed contribution of overcoming the limitations of linear CBMs.

Interpretability is not convincingly evaluated. The only explanation evidence consists of a few hand-selected CLEVR-Hans examples whose concept extractor is already aligned with the synthetic generative attributes. There is no quantitative concept quality, faithfulness, stability, human evaluation, or natural-image explanation analysis. Sparse CLIP similarities from a vocabulary of frequent LAION phrases are not automatically human-interpretable concepts.

The shortcut evidence does not isolate a general robustness benefit. It covers only CLEVR-Hans with one concept extractor and compares validation and test sets that differ in shortcut prevalence. At 0% clean data on CLEVR-Hans3, NCV has a larger gap and lower test accuracy than the nonlinear CBM; on CLEVR-Hans7 its gap is also worse than the linear CBM. The broad conclusion that NCV intrinsically mitigates shortcut learning is stronger than these mixed results support.

Claims of scalability and efficiency are unsupported by runtime, memory, convergence, or training-cost measurements. The approach trains three nonlinear agents, and the paper itself acknowledges greater cost and instability. Poor Pixel-MAC accuracy alone does not demonstrate computational scalability.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite many listed hyperparameters. The precise modified Morgana loss is relegated to a citation, differentiable hard top-k optimization and rejection-class training are insufficiently specified, construction of the non-confounded datasets is not documented, and no code or artifact availability statement is given. The references also contain an unresolved placeholder (“arXiv:2401.xxxxx”), indicating inadequate manuscript preparation.

Originality is modest: the method primarily composes existing concept extractors with the existing Merlin-Arthur classifier, without a new objective, theoretical result, or clear technical mechanism beyond changing the feature space. This could still be useful empirically, but the current ablations do not establish what the composition itself contributes.

The ethics discussion notes inherited CLIP bias but does not examine how misleading concept labels, rejection behavior, or false assurances of verification could affect the high-stakes deployments repeatedly invoked by the paper. These risks are especially relevant given that the central guarantees have not been demonstrated.

strengths: Originality/significance: NCV is a promising synthesis of concept representations and Merlin-Arthur-style prover-verifier training. Moving the interaction from pixels to concepts is intuitive, potentially useful, and addresses a genuine limitation of pixel-level explanations.

Empirical breadth: the evaluation spans controlled compositional datasets and large natural-image benchmarks. Reporting results over 20 seeds for CLEVR-Hans and 10 seeds for CIFAR-100/ImageNet is stronger than typical practice, and the appendix includes mask-size and selector-architecture ablations.

Predictive results are encouraging: NCV substantially outperforms Pixel-MAC on CIFAR-100 and ImageNet and improves over the concept baseline on both CLEVR-Hans datasets and CIFAR-100. The shortcut experiments also show competitive clean-test accuracy, especially once small amounts of unconfounded data are introduced.

Presentation: the paper is generally well organized, motivates the problem clearly, and provides readable diagrams and tables. The qualitative CLEVR examples communicate the intended advantage over diffuse pixel masks effectively.

Limitations and ethics: the discussion appropriately acknowledges dependence on concept quality, training instability and cost, divergence from expert semantics, and inherited CLIP biases. These are relevant limitations rather than reasons to penalize the work by themselves.
weaknesses: Soundness: the central claims of formal verifiability, certification, and faithful reasoning are not established. The paper provides no new theorem or applicable information-theoretic bound for its multiclass setting and explicitly states in the conclusion that extending existing binary guarantees to high-dimensional multiclass problems remains open. Empirical performance against a jointly trained Morgana is not a certificate against stronger or adaptive provers.

The reported soundness metric can count rejection as success, making near-100% scores difficult to interpret without rejection rates, coverage-risk curves, class-conditional results, or comparison against trivial rejection strategies. Moreover, the crucial modified Morgana loss is deferred to prior work and never specified, leaving unclear how the rejection class is trained and how the stated metric follows from the objective.

There is an unaddressed communication-channel failure mode: Merlin observes the complete concept vector, and Arthur can infer information from which coordinates are selected. The mask pattern itself can therefore encode the class even when the selected concepts do not semantically justify it. This is especially concerning with dense CLIP similarities, where selected versus zeroed coordinates are readily detectable. No label-randomization, mask-only, concept-intervention, or semantic-alignment test rules out this explanation.

The interpretability evidence is too limited for the paper's claims. Q3 relies on a few selected CLEVR-Hans examples whose underlying rules and NCB slots are unusually clean; there is no quantitative concept fidelity evaluation, human study, systematic comparison, or natural-image explanation analysis. Sparse concept names are not by themselves evidence that the decision is understandable or faithful.

Several comparisons confound the claimed benefit of prover-verifier training with representation, architecture, and information-budget differences. On natural images, NCV uses dense CLIP similarities and a nonlinear MLP, whereas the stated CBM uses sparse SpLiCE encodings; Pixel-MAC receives extremely restrictive pixel budgets that are not information-matched to 32 high-level concepts. A nonlinear CBM using exactly the same dense concepts, verifier architecture, training budget, and top-k sparsity is missing from the main benchmark.

The paper does not substantiate computational scalability: it reports neither training time, memory, convergence behavior, nor compute relative to Pixel-MAC and CBMs. Avoiding per-example SpLiCE optimization is plausible, but three-agent training for 100 epochs on ImageNet is not demonstrated to be efficient.

The shortcut conclusion is overstated. On CLEVR-Hans7 with 0% clean samples, NCV's validation-test gap is worse than the linear CBM's; on CLEVR-Hans3 it is worse than both CBM variants and has lower clean-test accuracy than the nonlinear CBM. Improvements with clean data are promising, but they do not establish intrinsic shortcut mitigation or generalize beyond one synthetic benchmark.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite useful hyperparameter details: there is no code or environment specification, exact split construction and concept vocabulary are not supplied, the differentiable hard top-k mechanism and optimization schedule are underspecified, and the appendix describes a nominally linear natural-image CBM while also mentioning a 512-unit hidden layer. These ambiguities impede faithful reproduction.

Overall, the idea and accuracy results have merit, but the unsupported verification/faithfulness claims and confounded baselines affect the paper's central contribution rather than merely its scope. A revised evaluation that closes the mask-channel loophole, reports rejection-aware robustness, and compares against matched nonlinear concept baselines could make the work substantially stronger.

strengths: The paper presents a coherent and potentially useful integration of Merlin-Arthur prover-verifier training with concept representations, enabling experiments on substantially larger image benchmarks than prior pixel-level PVGs.

The empirical study covers synthetic and natural-image datasets, includes linear and nonlinear CBMs, Pixel-MAC, and ResNet baselines, and generally reports results over 10 or 20 random seeds. Mask-size and gamma ablations, computational costs, and extensive optimization details are also provided.

The manuscript is well organized and clearly distinguishes completeness from soundness. The appendix is unusually candid that the original theory is binary, that the multiclass extension is only a one-vs-rest lens, and that AFC and adversary-strength assumptions are neither measured nor verified.
The shortcut experiments show a useful empirical pattern: when even 1% clean data is available, NCV improves clean-test accuracy and the validation-test gap relative to the evaluated CBMs.
Limitations related to concept-extractor quality, training instability, divergence from expert semantics, and inherited CLIP/LAION biases are acknowledged.
weaknesses: Soundness is presented as a strong guarantee or certificate, but the reported quantity only measures failure against one learned Morgana and counts abstention as success. No abstention rate, coverage-risk curve, attack from alternative or restarted adversaries, or exhaustive subset evaluation is reported. Near-100% soundness can therefore be achieved by rejecting Morgana's subsets without establishing robustness to admissible concept subsets.

The formal results do not support the central multiclass claims. The cited MAC result assumes binary classification, bounded AFC, controlled class imbalance, and sufficient relative adversary strength. NCV does not estimate these quantities; ImageNet one-vs-rest tasks are extremely imbalanced; and architectural symmetry is not evidence that Morgana has relative success rate near one. Moreover, the main tables report aggregate multiclass completeness and soundness rather than the class-conditional errors appearing in the bound. The appendix admits that the theory is only qualitative, which conflicts with repeated claims of formal, provable, and certifiable verifiability in the main paper.

Interpretability is not convincingly evaluated. Evidence consists mainly of a few hand-selected qualitative examples, with no human evaluation, concept precision/coherence measurement, intervention test, or comparison at matched sparsity. For ImageNet, the displayed explanation is the five most frequent concepts across 32 samples although the actual per-example certificate contains 32 concepts, which does not demonstrate concise per-instance interpretability.

The mask pattern itself is a high-capacity communication channel: selecting 32 positions from a 10,000-dimensional vocabulary can encode class identity even if selected concept values are not semantically evidential. No control using shuffled concept names/values, fixed or class-independent masks, or analysis of mask-label information rules out this failure mode. This is especially important because exact subset reuse is acknowledged to be rare, making the inherited containment-based interpretation difficult to apply.

The evidence does not isolate the benefit of the proposed PVG. The frozen CLIP/NCB representation performs most of the dimensionality reduction, and there is no matched sparse concept-selector baseline without Morgana. The pretrained nonlinear verifier reaches 85.96% on CIFAR-100, 77.07% on ImageNet, and 81.39% on COCOLogic, whereas NCV obtains 83.32%, 67.04%, and 75.42%, respectively. These results suggest a substantial accuracy cost from NCV, while the lower nonlinear-CBM numbers in Table 1 are insufficiently reconciled with the appendix's stronger pretrained-verifier results.

Several comparisons are not well controlled. Pixel-MAC uses a ResNet-18 on natural-image tasks while the black-box baseline uses ResNet-50, and pixel budgets vary considerably by resolution. The DCR implementation learns concepts through an unpretrained ResNet-18 supervised by CLIP similarities, whereas NCV directly consumes precomputed CLIP similarities, so its large performance gap is not an apples-to-apples comparison.

The shortcut conclusion is overstated: with 0% clean data, NCV has a worse validation-test gap than the nonlinear CBM on CLEVR-Hans3, and the experiments do not establish that gains arise from adversarial prover-verifier training rather than architecture, capacity, or optimization differences.

The description of the stabilizing term is mathematically inconsistent: the stated term -log(1+exp(-|z_y-z_reject|)) increases toward zero as the absolute logit gap grows, so maximizing Morgana's loss encourages rather than discourages large separation. This casts doubt on the claimed interpretation of the training objective.

Reproducibility is only partial. Many hyperparameters and hardware estimates are supplied, but no code or artifact availability is stated, and exact vocabulary construction, preprocessing, dataset splits, checkpoint selection, and full evaluation implementation are not sufficiently specified. Ethical discussion notes inherited foundation-model bias but does not analyze how misleading concept names or abstention behavior could affect the suggested high-stakes use cases.

strengths: The paper is clearly organized and motivates a sensible combination of concept representations with prover-verifier training. The modularity across NCB and CLIP-based representations is appealing. The evaluation spans synthetic and natural-image datasets, uses multiple seeds, and includes useful mask-size, adversarial-weight, runtime, and shortcut-correlation studies.

Some predictive results are promising, particularly the reported CIFAR-100 and COCOLogic completeness and the improved clean-test accuracy when small amounts of non-confounded CLEVR-Hans data are available.

The limitations discussion is unusually candid about dependence on concept quality, inherited CLIP biases, optimization instability, multiclass imbalance, rare feature-containment events, and the restricted neural adversary.
Research-ethics concerns are acknowledged through discussion of pretrained-model bias and expert-semantic mismatch, and the use of language models is disclosed.
weaknesses: The central claim of formal or certifiable verifiability is not supported by the presented results. The inherited theorem is binary and requires bounded asymmetric feature correlation, class imbalance, and a sufficiently strong adversary; the paper estimates none of these quantities. Its multiclass one-vs-rest extension is only a qualitative lens, and Appendix A explicitly concedes that the experiments do not provide quantitative certificates.

The reported near-100% soundness is potentially trivial because a Morgana example counts as sound whenever Arthur is correct or abstains, while the training objective explicitly encourages abstention. The paper reports neither rejection rates nor coverage-conditional error or risk-coverage curves. A verifier that rejects every adversarial subset would score perfect soundness, so these numbers do not establish robust verification.

The most relevant matched comparison undermines the performance narrative: the verifier trained directly on full CLIP-Sim features obtains 85.96% on CIFAR-100, 77.07% on ImageNet, and 81.39% on COCOLogic (Table 8), whereas NCV reaches only 83.32%, 67.04%, and 75.42% (Table 1). Comparisons against linear and nonlinear CBMs instead use sparse SpLiCE features, confounding the effect of the prover-verifier game with the representation. Thus the claimed closing of the interpretability-accuracy gap is not isolated experimentally.

The Pixel-MAC comparison is insufficient to establish scalability. It uses a ResNet-18 even on ImageNet while other image baselines use ResNet-50 and NCV benefits from pretrained CLIP representations. Pixel and concept mask budgets are also semantically incomparable. The very weak ImageNet Pixel-MAC result may therefore reflect the chosen implementation rather than an inherent limitation of pixel-space PVGs.

Interpretability is supported almost entirely by a few selected qualitative examples. There is no human study, concept-precision evaluation, class-rule recovery metric, stability analysis, or comparison against strong concept-attribution methods. The ImageNet explanation is aggregated across 32 samples and contains awkward vocabulary items, making it weak evidence for per-instance human interpretability.

The shortcut-mitigation conclusion is overstated. With 0% clean data, NCV is worse than the nonlinear CBM on CLEVR-Hans3 test accuracy and validation-test gap, and worse on the gap for CLEVR-Hans7. Improvements appear only after clean samples are introduced, without a sufficiently controlled ablation separating PVG training from model capacity, regularization, or checkpoint selection.

Empirical soundness is measured only against the jointly trained Morgana network. Symmetric architecture does not demonstrate comparable search strength, and there is no exhaustive subset search on small problems, stronger post-hoc attacker, or transfer attack. Consequently, failure of this adversary cannot be interpreted as robustness to arbitrary misleading concept subsets.

The DCR comparison is difficult to regard as fair: DCR is trained with a separate ResNet-18 and dense supervision toward 10,000 CLIP similarities, whereas NCV directly consumes precomputed CLIP features. Reporting a timeout under this substantially different pipeline does not isolate NCV's scalability advantage.

Originality is modest: the main contribution is a relatively direct composition of existing Merlin-Arthur training with existing concept extractors, without a new theorem. Given the unsupported verification claims and confounded evaluation, the current evidence is not strong enough for others to rely on the proposed method.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite extensive hyperparameter reporting: no code or artifact is provided, and details needed to reconstruct alternating optimization, continuous-mask parameterization, preprocessing, checkpoint selection, and exact concept extraction are missing or ambiguous. The omission is especially important for a reportedly unstable three-player game.

strengths: Originality/significance: NCV is a useful synthesis of concept representations and Merlin-Arthur prover-verifier training. Moving the game from pixels to a 10,000-concept space is practically motivated and could make PVG-style methods applicable to substantially larger vision problems.

Soundness/empirical scope: The evaluation spans synthetic and natural-image datasets, including ImageNet-1k, and generally reports many random seeds. The mask-size and gamma ablations, shortcut experiments, runtime comparisons, and explicit Pixel-MAC baseline provide useful evidence about optimization behavior and scalability.

The paper reports strong predictive results in several settings: 83.32% on CIFAR-100 and 75.42% on COCOLogic, with large gains over the reported linear CBMs and Pixel-MAC. The CLEVR-Hans experiments also show that sparse concept selection can preserve high accuracy.

Presentation: The method and alternating optimization procedure are explained clearly, figures are legible, and the supplementary material gives substantial architectural, optimization, hardware, and runtime detail.

Limitations/ethics: The authors candidly state that the inherited Merlin-Arthur theory is only an idealized lens here, identify the unverified adversary-strength and feature-correlation assumptions, and discuss concept quality and inherited CLIP biases. This honesty is valuable and should not itself be penalized.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central claims of “formal verifiability,” “guarantees,” and “certifiable decision-making” are not established for the evaluated models. The inherited theorem is binary and depends on bounded asymmetric feature correlation, class balance, and Morgana's relative success; none of these quantities is measured. The paper concedes that exact selected subsets may have negligible probability and that its results are not quantitative certificates, which conflicts with stronger claims in the abstract, main text, and conclusion.

The reported soundness metric counts both correct predictions and rejection as successes, but the paper never reports Morgana-side rejection rate, correct-class rate, or coverage. Near-100% soundness can therefore result from Arthur simply abstaining on almost every adversarial subset. Without a risk-coverage or rejection decomposition, the headline soundness results provide weak evidence of useful robustness.

The most important same-representation control is effectively omitted from Table 1. Table 8 shows that the pretrained nonlinear CLIP-Sim verifier without PVG achieves 85.96%, 77.07%, and 81.39% on CIFAR-100, ImageNet-1k, and COCOLogic, respectively, whereas NCV achieves only 83.32%, 67.04%, and 75.42%. Thus PVG training decreases accuracy relative to its own initialization on every natural-image dataset. Comparisons against weaker or differently represented CBMs do not isolate the benefit of NCV.

Baseline comparability is unclear. NCV uses dense CLIP-Sim features while the CBM is described as using optimized sparse SpLiCE encodings; the supposedly linear CBM description also states that a 512-unit hidden layer is used. Pixel-MAC employs a different backbone and manually selected pixel budgets. These inconsistencies and confounds weaken the claimed accuracy and efficiency advantages.

Interpretability is supported almost entirely by a few hand-selected qualitative examples. There is no concept-quality metric, human evaluation, stability analysis, faithfulness intervention, or comparison at matched sparsity. Because the prover observes the entire encoding, it can also communicate class information through the pattern of selected indices rather than select semantically valid evidence. Some displayed ImageNet concepts are themselves noisy, such as “extend,” “support,” and “cappuchino.”

The shortcut evidence does not establish intrinsic mitigation. With 0% clean data, NCV has a larger validation-test gap than the nonlinear CBM on CLEVR-Hans3 and only improves once clean examples are introduced. A controlled ablation against the same pretrained verifier and concept representation, ideally with explicit shortcut-concept selection statistics, is needed.

Reproducibility is only partial: many hyperparameters and runtimes are supplied, but no code or artifact availability is stated, some dataset/split details are underspecified, and the unusual Morgana loss and continuous-to-hard mask procedure would be difficult to reproduce reliably from prose alone. Ethical limitations of pretrained concept vocabularies are acknowledged, but no empirical bias assessment is performed. Overall, the idea is promising, but the missing abstention analysis, same-backbone controls, and quantitative interpretability evidence prevent reliable validation of the central claims.
